title: Sigmoid volvulus: management and deterioration

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee on call. An 81-year-old man from a care home has two days of progressive abdominal distension, pain and no flatus. He is haemodynamically stable on arrival. The abdominal radiograph report describes a markedly dilated, inverted-U-shaped sigmoid loop.
brief.task: Discuss diagnosis, investigation and treatment. The examiner will update you about the patient’s course.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Differentiate uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus from ischaemic or perforated bowel that requires urgent surgery.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating every volvulus with endoscopy even after new peritonism or shock.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Check stability, peritonism and bowel perfusion risk before deciding on endoscopic decompression.

flow: ABCDE, analgesia, IV access, fluids as indicated; assess peritonism and sepsis.
Interpret radiograph, consider CT where needed and involve senior colorectal team.
For stable uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus, organise urgent flexible sigmoidoscopic detorsion and mucosal assessment.
When perforation, ischaemia, failed endoscopy or instability appears, pivot to urgent operative management.
Plan recurrence prevention, ongoing monitoring and a documented patient/family explanation.

grid.label: Initial assessment
grid.fail: Treats abdominal distension as constipation without observations.
grid.borderline: Measures vital signs but overlooks abdominal tenderness and peritonism.
grid.pass: Assesses ABCDE, pain, observations and peritonism with IV access and fluids if needed.
grid.high: Anticipates frailty, dehydration and sepsis; allocates monitoring while planning definitive care.

grid.label: Diagnostic synthesis
grid.fail: Fails to identify large-bowel obstruction from symptoms and radiograph.
grid.borderline: Names obstruction but not the likely sigmoid twist.
grid.pass: Recognises probable sigmoid volvulus with obstruction and the typical radiographic pattern.
grid.high: Explains how sigmoid volvulus differs from pseudo-obstruction and caecal volvulus.

grid.label: Investigation and imaging
grid.fail: Assumes plain film excludes bowel ischaemia and needs no further assessment.
grid.borderline: Requests CT without considering instability or urgent senior review.
grid.pass: Requests appropriate bloods and CT when diagnosis/complications need clarification, without delaying resuscitation.
grid.high: Uses lactate and imaging as aids, not substitutes for serial examination or operative judgement.

grid.label: Uncomplicated decompression
grid.fail: Prescribes laxatives alone for suspected sigmoid volvulus.
grid.borderline: Mentions endoscopy but no urgency or mucosal assessment.
grid.pass: Arranges urgent flexible sigmoidoscopy detorsion for stable uncomplicated disease and assesses mucosal viability.
grid.high: Adds post-detorsion drainage strategy per team and early recurrence prevention discussion.

grid.label: Signs requiring surgery
grid.fail: Offers endoscopy despite rigidity, shock and suspected perforation.
grid.borderline: Notes increasing pain but does not change plan.
grid.pass: Identifies peritonitis, suspected ischaemia, perforation or failed decompression as indications for urgent surgery.
grid.high: Explains risk of non-viable colon and need for senior-led resection/stoma decisions.

grid.label: Resuscitation and antibiotics
grid.fail: Leaves shocked patient untreated while arranging routine endoscopy.
grid.borderline: Provides fluids but fails to manage suspected intra-abdominal sepsis.
grid.pass: When shocked/peritonitic, organises senior/anaesthetic support, IV fluids, bloods including group and crossmatch, and IV antibiotics as appropriate.
grid.high: Coordinates sepsis care and urgent source control, with catheter for urine-output assessment.

grid.label: Differential diagnoses
grid.fail: States all large-bowel dilation should be treated identically.
grid.borderline: Lists pseudo-obstruction without describing different initial management.
grid.pass: Contrasts sigmoid volvulus, pseudo-obstruction and mechanical malignant obstruction.
grid.high: Notes that caecal volvulus generally requires operative management, unlike uncomplicated sigmoid detorsion.

grid.label: Recurrence and follow-up
grid.fail: Discharges after detorsion with no recurrence or definitive-treatment plan (major omission).
grid.borderline: Mentions recurrence but no colorectal review.
grid.pass: Discusses high recurrence risk and specialist consideration of definitive surgery when fit.
grid.high: Frames individualised decision around frailty, goals of care and definitive risk reduction.

grid.label: Communication
grid.fail: Tells family endoscopy is always curative and risk-free.
grid.borderline: Explains blockage but not deterioration signals or options.
grid.pass: Explains the twist, proposed endoscopy if stable, and possible surgery if complications arise.
grid.high: Rechecks capacity/preferences, provides clear risk-benefit counselling and handover.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: An 81-year-old has distension, no flatus and a large inverted-U sigmoid loop. What is your assessment?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: He is constipated. I will prescribe senna without checking for peritonism.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It does not look like an obstruction to me.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The film is enough to prove there is no bowel compromise.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He is still stable. How would you manage the apparent twist?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will give laxatives and wait overnight.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He now becomes tachycardic, hypotensive and rigid.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will still book flexible sigmoidoscopy tomorrow.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I do not think he needs antibiotics or senior review yet.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What else can dilate the colon?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It makes no difference; all large-bowel dilatation is treated the same way.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: His daughter asks if this will come back.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, once we untwist it, it is permanently cured.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: She asks whether the camera test is safe.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It always cures the problem and carries no risk at all.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: An 81-year-old has two days of distension, pain and no flatus. Please assess.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I am the core surgical trainee. I will obtain observations, perform ABCDE and abdominal examination for peritonism, assess hydration, give appropriate analgesia, get IV access and inform the senior surgical team.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: BP 132/78, pulse 88, temperature 37.1°C; very distended, tympanitic, mildly tender, no guarding.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Together with the radiographic inverted-U sigmoid loop, this suggests sigmoid volvulus causing large-bowel obstruction.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: FBC, U&Es, CRP, venous gas/lactate, and CT abdomen/pelvis if needed to clarify diagnosis or assess complications. Reassessment is essential.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will arrange urgent flexible sigmoidoscopy to detorse and decompress, assess mucosal viability and discuss a decompression tube with the endoscopy/colorectal team.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What if there is perforation or non-viable bowel?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: No endoscopic detorsion then; urgent senior colorectal surgery assessment for operative source control is required.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: He now becomes hypotensive, rigid and febrile.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is likely ischaemia or perforation. I will escalate immediately, resuscitate with IV fluids, take bloods including crossmatch, start IV antibiotics for suspected intra-abdominal sepsis, insert a urinary catheter for output and prepare urgently for theatre.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What else can dilate the colon?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction and obstructing cancer are differentials; caecal volvulus also has a different operative approach.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Recurrence is common; I would discuss elective definitive sigmoid resection with the colorectal team depending on fitness and patient preferences.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: His daughter asks why he might need an operation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The bowel has twisted. If the bowel becomes damaged or perforates, an operation may be lifesaving. We will explain options and risks clearly.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Your patient has severe distension and no flatus. Lead the assessment.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will check for shock and peritonitis first because they determine whether endoscopy is safe. Please provide observations; I will assess ABCDE, examine for guarding, establish IV access and get senior colorectal input.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: BP 132/78, pulse 88, temperature 37.1°C; distended, tympanitic, mild tenderness, no guarding.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The radiograph description of a markedly dilated inverted-U sigmoid loop is characteristic of sigmoid volvulus. Obstruction is likely, but I still need to exclude non-viable bowel.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Check haemoglobin, inflammatory markers, renal function, electrolytes and lactate. CT can clarify the twist and complications when appropriate, while serial examination and surgical judgement remain central.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What is the first definitive step while he is stable?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Urgent flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression by the appropriate team, assessing the mucosa for ischaemia, with decompression-tube planning where appropriate. I would discuss the high recurrence risk early.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What would make that plan unsafe?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: New guarding or rigidity, haemodynamic instability, perforation or clear ischaemia, or failed endoscopy. In those circumstances I would stop the endoscopic route and prepare for emergency surgery.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He develops BP 86/50, fever 38.6°C and a rigid abdomen.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This has changed to a probable strangulated or perforated bowel with sepsis. I am calling the consultant colorectal surgeon and anaesthetics now. Give IV resuscitation with close reassessment, IV antibiotics per local intra-abdominal sepsis policy, urgent bloods, group and crossmatch, and urinary catheter to monitor perfusion. Prepare theatre without delay.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That causes dilation without a mechanical twist. It has a separate assessment and stepwise management pathway; caecal volvulus is also not approached with routine flexible sigmoid detorsion.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: We would address nutrition and physiology, and jointly consider planned sigmoid resection during the appropriate admission/interval because recurrence after detorsion is frequent. Fitness and goals of care matter.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: His daughter is frightened by mention of a stoma.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would explain that we hope to relieve the obstruction, but if the bowel has become dead or perforated, resection—and sometimes a stoma—may be necessary. The consultant will explain the operative choices, and we will consider the patient’s wishes.

failures.move: Performs endoscopic detorsion despite frank peritonitis
failures.consequence: perforation/ischaemia may worsen and surgery is delayed.

failures.move: Does not resuscitate or give appropriate antibiotics in septic shock
Does not assess observations or peritonism
failures.consequence: misses a transition to complicated volvulus.

recovery.when: If new rigidity and hypotension change the situation
recovery.line: The new rigidity and hypotension change the situation: endoscopic detorsion is no longer my plan. I will escalate immediately for operative assessment and resuscitate.

recovery.when: If you mentioned pseudo-obstruction without distinguishing it
recovery.line: I mentioned pseudo-obstruction but should distinguish it: this radiographic twist suggests mechanical sigmoid volvulus and requires a different pathway.

knowledge.fact: Uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus can be treated with urgent flexible or rigid sigmoidoscopic detorsion.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy also assesses mucosal viability.
Sigmoid volvulus may present with obstruction or perforation/peritonitis.
Peritonitis, ischaemia and non-viable bowel require urgent operative rather than routine endoscopic management.
Caecal volvulus differs: colonoscopic reduction is not recommended as routine treatment.
Recurrence after endoscopic detorsion is common (45–71%); WSES recommends sigmoid colectomy as early as possible, even during the index admission, if the patient is fit.

recall.think: Twisted sigmoid bowel: first decide stable versus peritonitic.
recall.say: Stable without peritonitis: urgent endoscopic detorsion; unstable or peritonitic: surgeon and theatre.
do: Resuscitate, investigate, examine repeatedly and select the appropriate source-control path.

numbers.meaning: No single fixed pressure/lactate threshold determines surgery here; clinical shock or peritonism is decisive.

recall.trap: Do not continue endoscopy when rigidity or shock develops.
recall.finish: Plan recurrence prevention and explain potential resection or stoma.

partner.opening: Eighty-one-year-old with distension, pain and obstipation; x-ray has a dilated inverted-U sigmoid loop.

reveals.trigger: Only reveal initial stable observations when candidate requests them
reveals.finding: BP 132/78, pulse 88, temperature 37.1°C; very distended, tympanitic, mildly tender, no guarding. No peritonism initially.

push.question: Daughter’s stoma concern arises only in the communication segment.

curveballs.prompt: ask about viability/perforation criteria after uncomplicated management.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Identifies peritonitis, suspected ischaemia, perforation or failed decompression as indications for urgent surgery.

curveballs.prompt: new fever 38.6°C, BP 86/50 and rigid abdomen
curveballs.safeAnswer: candidate must abandon endoscopy and activate resuscitation/operative pathway.
